questions.question: A travel guide says that a desert town has a dry climate. Ana visits on a day of pouring rain, with water rushing down the streets. What does the rainy day show?
questions.answer: One day's weather can differ from the climate
choices: One day's weather can differ from the climate
The town's climate has turned from dry to wet
The guide was wrong to call the climate dry
Deserts get as much rain as other places
questions.context: Weather is the state of the air at one place and time; climate is a place's usual weather, averaged over 30 years or more. A desert gets very little rain in most years, so a rare storm, even one that floods the streets, leaves its climate as dry as before.
questions.grade_note: Texas's 2017 grade 5 standard 112.16(b)(8)(A) asks students to 'differentiate between weather and climate', and a desert on a rainy day is the scope's own example.

questions.question: On a muggy summer morning the air feels damp and sticky, because it holds a great deal of invisible water vapour. What is the amount of water vapour in the air called?
questions.context: Humidity is the water vapour in the air, often given as a percentage, and an instrument called a hygrometer measures it. Precipitation is water falling from clouds as rain, snow, sleet or hail, and air pressure is the push of the air's weight.
questions.grade_note: Florida's grade 5 benchmark SC.5.E.7.3 names humidity among the factors that determine the weather, and its lesson has it measured with a hygrometer.

questions.question: The air above a weather station stretches many kilometres up, and all of it presses down on the ground below. Which instrument measures this push of the air, called air pressure?
questions.context: A barometer measures air pressure, the weight of all the air above pressing down. Weather watchers read it because the pressure rises and falls as the weather changes. A thermometer measures temperature, an anemometer wind speed, and a rain gauge rainfall.
questions.grade_note: Florida's grade 5 lesson for SC.5.E.7.3 teaches barometric pressure as the weight of the atmosphere pushing down, 'measured with a tool called a barometer'.

questions.question: At the top of a pole at a weather station, three or four small cups sit on short arms, free to spin round. What does this instrument measure?
questions.context: It is an anemometer. The wind catches the cups and spins them, and the stronger the wind, the faster they turn, so their turning gives the wind's speed. The cups hold no water: a rain gauge collects rain, and a wind vane shows the wind's direction.
questions.grade_note: Florida's grade 5 lesson for SC.5.E.7.3 has wind speed measured with an anemometer, and NOAA's student weather station builds a cup anemometer.

questions.question: A wind vane on a barn roof swings round in a breeze, then holds steady, its arrow pointing one way. What does the arrow's point show?
questions.answer: Where the wind is coming from
choices: Where the wind is coming from
Where the wind is going to
questions.context: A wind vane's arrow turns to point into the wind, toward the direction it blows from. Winds are named the same way: a north wind blows from the north toward the south. The letters N, E, S and W fixed below the arrow show the compass directions.
questions.grade_note: Florida's grade 5 benchmark SC.5.E.7.3 covers wind direction, which its lesson says 'is measured as the direction the wind is blowing from', and NOAA's student weather vane points that way.

questions.question: An airliner climbs through a thick white cloud and comes out into bright sunshine above it. What is the cloud made of?
questions.answer: Tiny drops of water or ice
choices: Tiny drops of water or ice
Water vapour, a kind of gas
questions.context: A cloud is a crowd of drops of water, or bits of ice, so tiny that they float in the air. Water vapour is an invisible gas, so it cannot be seen; a cloud forms where the vapour turns into drops, and the drops are what make it look white.
questions.grade_note: NSTA's probe 'What Are Clouds Made Of?' targets this idea, and a study of 300 fifth graders (Alkis 2007) found about 42 percent called the water vapour in the air a cloud.

questions.question: On a warm, sunny afternoon, white clouds with flat bottoms and puffy, rounded tops drift over a park like heaps of cotton. What kind of cloud are they?
questions.context: Cumulus clouds form when the Sun warms the ground and warm, damp air rises, and their name is Latin for 'heap'. Small ones like these are fair-weather clouds, but on some days a cumulus keeps growing into a towering cumulonimbus, the thunderstorm cloud.
questions.grade_note: GLOBE's K-5 cloud activity has learners recognise and name the three main kinds (cirrus, cumulus, stratus) by look, and the curriculum map's grade 5 line G5.E8 places them here.

questions.question: A low, flat sheet of grey cloud covers the whole sky over a town all day, and a light drizzle falls from it. What kind of cloud is it?
questions.context: Stratus clouds spread across the sky in an even grey layer, and their name comes from Latin for 'spread out'. They bring dull days and drizzle, and a stratus cloud resting on the ground is fog. A cumulonimbus brings heavy rain and thunder instead.
questions.grade_note: GLOBE's K-5 cloud activity has learners recognise and name the three main kinds (cirrus, cumulus, stratus) by look, and Pennsylvania's eligible content S4.D.2.1.1 asks students to identify cirrus, cumulus, stratus and cumulonimbus.

questions.question: A weather report says that cirrus clouds will cross the sky this afternoon. What will they look like?
questions.answer: Thin white wisps high in the sky
choices: Thin white wisps high in the sky
Puffy white heaps with flat bottoms
A flat grey sheet low over the land
Dark towers that flash with lightning
questions.context: Cirrus clouds float more than 6 kilometres up, where the air is so cold that they are made of ice crystals; their name is Latin for 'curl of hair'. Puffy heaps are cumulus, a flat grey sheet is stratus, and lightning comes from cumulonimbus.
questions.grade_note: GLOBE's K-5 cloud activity asks learners to describe the look and typical heights of cirrus, cumulus and stratus, and the curriculum map's grade 5 line G5.E8 places them here.

questions.question: On a hot, sunny afternoon at the beach, a steady wind begins to blow in from the sea toward the land. Why does this sea breeze blow?
questions.answer: The Sun warms the land faster than the sea
choices: The Sun warms the land faster than the sea
The Sun warms the sea faster than the land
The waves push the air toward the shore
The tide pulls the air in with the water
questions.context: Sunshine heats sand and soil faster than water. The warm air over the land rises, and cooler air from over the sea flows in to take its place, while waves and tides play no part. At night the land cools faster, and the breeze turns round to blow out to sea.
questions.grade_note: A Texas grade 5 lesson for TEKS 5.10A (how the Sun and the ocean affect weather) teaches that sea breezes come from land and water heating at different rates.
